ingenious

/in-JEEN-yuhs/ - the stress falls on JEEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ingenious means cleverly inventive, creating something new to solve a problem.

The museum's ingenious rainy-day pass — half price, valid only while it pours — fills the quietest galleries all winter.

Example

The architect's one ingenious idea paid the apartment's whole rent: staircase drawers. Every tread pulls open — winter boots in the bottom step, tax papers at the turn, the cat's supplies at the top — fourteen drawers hiding inside a staircase that had wasted that space for a century. Visitors climb it twice before they believe it.

Ingenious is the exact word because the design is cleverly inventive and resourceful — a genuinely new answer, not just a competent one. Clever praises the mind in general; ingenious points at the invention itself, the trick nobody had thought to build. If the solution makes people ask why no one did this before, ingenious is waiting.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

resourceful: Resourceful praises making do with whatever is already on hand — repurposing, improvising, pressing nearby things into service. Ingenious goes further: it invents something genuinely new, a trick or device nobody had thought to try. Resourceful stretches the existing; ingenious adds to it.

imaginative: Imaginative means full of new images and fancies, useful or not — an invented creature, a daydreamed city. The word praises the mental picture itself, not the working result. Ingenious keeps the newness but demands that the new idea actually solve a problem in the world.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

predictable: offering only the obvious answer anyone would expect

uninspired: competent, and instantly forgettable

Where it sits · how far past ordinary the solution goes

clever → ingenious → revolutionary

clever vs. ingenious: A clever fix does the job neatly; an ingenious one does it in a way nobody thought possible.

revolutionary vs. ingenious: Revolutionary goes past ingenious — the invention doesn't just solve its problem, it rewrites how the whole field works.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: in, within

Root — geni: inborn talent (Latin gignere, to be born)

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together: In- (within) + geni- (inborn talent, from gignere, "to be born") + -ous (full of) = full of inborn talent. Latin ingenium was the cleverness you were born carrying. The Romans would have said the staircase architect had ingenium to spare — invention flowing from native wit. Genius grows from the same root; so, by a trick of history, does ingenuous, the near-twin that means innocently frank, which is why the two are worth keeping apart.

Use the root in a new word: genius: The bridge's designer earned a reputation for genius after solving in one sketch a problem that had stalled the city's engineers for a decade.

Word Choice

neutral / admiring

Ingenious is applause for the invention itself — reach for it when the answer is new, not merely competent. Its neighbor resourceful praises making do with what's on hand: the camper who splints a tent pole with a spoon is resourceful; the architect who hides fourteen drawers in a staircase is ingenious. And keep this unit's canny apart: canny reads a situation shrewdly; ingenious builds something that wasn't there. (Beware ingenuous — one letter away, meaning innocently frank.)
